Interviewer:	I'll tell you a bit about what we're doing. We're interviewing women engineers, across the departments – all people in their 2nd year, we're mainly interviewing people that are going on placement – are you going on placement?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Oh right, OK. And we're looking at women's experiences of their education so far and why they've decided to do engineering and what they expect to get from their placement – and we're hoping to go back to people when they're on their placement and see whether it is what they really expected – things like that. What we're trying to do is see whether they're might be any discrepancies in expectations and reality and we aim to try and improve women's retention in the engineering industry. It's a 2 year project, and, at the end of that, we're going to put together a document that we'll give to the engineering council and engineering companies, hopefully, to improve the situation for women in the industry. That's basically what we're doing. I'll start off asking you a few questions about background things and why you decided to go into engineering, if that's OK. Is it mechanical engineering that you're doing?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	I did maths, physics, biology and French.

Interviewer:	What type of school did you go to?

Subject:	I went to a – a comprehensive – it was a Church of England school (right) fairly small, about 4 or 500 students in total. Er, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got any previous work experience?

Subject:	No, I haven't – not in the engineering industry anyway. I've done it in my school's mix.

Interviewer:	OK, what do your parents do? Are either of them engineers?

Subject:	Erm, my mum isn't – not at all. She's more into financial stuff, but she's retired now. She was like a clerical assistant. My dad works for the local council, but he's previously studied up to HNC level in electrical engineering and electronics. So…

Interviewer:	OK, so when and why do you think you did decide to study engineering?

Subject:	Er, I think I did it partly because no one else was really doing it at the time. I thought it might be quite interesting, and it's quite broad – I didn't want to limit my options, at the time. What else? I think I liked the fact that it had a design side to it, I thought it might be a different way of getting into design and understanding it from a different point of view, and hopefully become a better designer. That's my theory anyway.

Interviewer:	OK, were your family very supportive and things like that?

Subject:	Yeah, I haven't had any problems with that.

Interviewer:	Did you have any careers advice while you were at school?

Subject:	Yeah, there was a careers service but they didn't really – they explained to me all the options but they didn't really have much influence on my choice at all.

Interviewer:	Did they tell you much about doing engineering?

Subject:	No, not really. It was one of those things I had to kind of look out for myself (yeah) and I think the reason – I got to sixth form, where I think my physics teacher, she's the one that really knew more about the wider organisations and stuff like that. But, previously, there hadn't been any information or promotion of it really.

Interviewer:	When do you think you realised that you were interested in engineering work – after you'd taken your A levels, or did you choose…

Subject:	I think it was before, because it was when I was choosing universities and course I could study, and let's see, I changed a couple of times basically 'cos I was looking at the subjects I could study – like I say, I thought I might find engineering a bit more interesting. So I changed my A levels slightly and changed college and then stuck with it from there, really.

Interviewer:	OK, did the fact that your dad had had some experience in the industry influence you at all?

Subject:	Erm, let's see. I suppose to some extent it might have, but at the moment I can't really – because it was a different side of engineering. I think his is more theoretical whereas mechanical's more – you get to see what exactly you're talking about. I suppose it was helpful in terms of the kinds of projects or things you might get involved in, so that's where it might have influenced it a little bit. But I think it's still a bit new to me, even though I'm in my second year of the degree. It's still quite a new subject.

Interviewer:	How and why did you decide to do mechanical engineering and not another part of engineering, like electrical or maybe civil?

Subject:	Erm, well seeing what my dad gets up to, kind of put me off electrical. It is interesting but the depth of it – I think I would have got a bit bored with it. Erm, civil – I'm interested in like buildings and construction but I really don't think I would have been interested in like drainage and road elements and all that. Er, what other types – chemical – chemistry I can only do to a point and then it's – it just doesn't happen or I don't get it. Erm, what other types are there? Manufacturing – thought it was a bit too specialist, at the time.

Interviewer:	Did you actually– consider all the others and rule them out before you did decide?

Subject:	Yeah, I did look at all of them and like looking at the University prospectuses to see what you can learn in the course, what modules you covered and I just felt that – I knew I didn't want to specialise too soon, especially not having any experience in the industry, it's a bit too early to say. Yeah – what – I had a tendency towards – I thought I'd keep it to the mechanical because it seemed to be the broadest or at least cover different aspects of each sort of engineering, so yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, when you started the degree, did you always know that you wanted to do the sandwich course?

Subject:	Er, no. I did put it down as an option. I decided to do the sandwich course, because not a lot of Universities offer it and I thought I don't know how I feel, but put it down, just in case I did, so…

Interviewer:	OK, when you were choosing universities was that something you looked at then?

Subject:	Yeah, I saw it as an advantage because obviously there's a link with industry and er like I suppose, after that year you might think – well obviously how you find the year as well, and er when you finish as well, you probably have a better awareness of industry. So you – that's why I kind of favoured the universities that did offer it, even though at the time I wasn't sure if I'd just go straight through the year, or actually do it.

Interviewer:	OK, erm, how then did you decide specifically to come to [this university]?

Subject:	Oh goodness. Well, I looked at all the information and the careers – well the subjects at the universities. I had a look at the league tables and also how industry had rated the tables because I know like there's certain – in industry there's certain universities favoured by industry. I looked at all that, went and had a look around a few and well basically, kept in mind the ones that rated quite highly, had a look round and saw which ones I felt I might, you know, get along in or be suited to. Er, what else? I'm just trying to think. Er, yeah, could you repeat the question again, so I can….

Interviewer:	How did you decide to come to [this university]?

Subject:	I was – I favoured the campus style as well, the fact of having everything there really. And then, I think I knew people that was coming that – they were not necessarily doing engineering, so I could get their opinion on the place. Er, I didn't just come in here and see what was here, I felt that – yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, when you started doing engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Erm, I think I knew it was. When I went on a visit to the places erm like when we went on a visit to [name] and places like that – you did realise but it wasn't a shock. It was like OK, so there's not many girls here, that was about it really.

Interviewer:	Yeah, it didn't bother you at all?

Subject:	No, not at all.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled to take engineering?

Subject:	Er, I don't – well, I think the opportunities are there really. Erm, 'cos obviously there's girls on the course and doing other types of engineering as well, but, to some extent I don't think it's for everyone, because a lot of girls – I don't like to stereotype but they tend to go for your medias, your sociology and things like that and engineering is probably seen as all you do is work and if you're – I don't know, if they're playing with Meccano sets or you know when you're little, it doesn't seem very girly. Erm, so, yeah I think because it's got a such a masculine tendency, even though there is – obviously the design and problem solving, which girls can equally do as boys but I think yeah, the impression is still a bit masculine, a bit (?). Not necessarily (?) tables and stuff because that's not necessarily true.

Interviewer:	Do you think that's what people think about the industry – being masculine and that? Do you think that is really true or is it just a perception?

Subject:	Erm, I don't know. There's definitely the male influence – yeah, it would be wrong saying things like that, but I think when I've gone on my placement I'll probably have a better idea because I haven't actually been in industrial environment. The only things I've been exposed to is seen on my course and obviously, some of the A levels that I did, like physics and maths were – there are a lot of boys there. Erm, and I must say that it really wasn't a problem. It really didn't matter you just get on and do it, and I don't know if that influence is always there, because I went to a mixed school but you just – you're not really bothered by the fact and – yeah.

Interviewer:	You said that when you had careers advice, that they didn't really mention engineering and you had to go and find out about it yourself. Do you think that having more information generally about what engineering is, at an earlier age would, not necessarily get more women into the industry, but at least give them an opportunity … and maybe even men as well?

Subject:	Yeah, I think definitely at a younger age, because like I said, there is the information out there and I only really got more of it when I was at sixth form, yeah? I think er let me see – well I think tasks that you would do, there's different projects that you could get involved in – definitely make children aware of it and they would kind of develop their interest from there. I think…

Interviewer:	Do you think that's important to do that with men and women?

Subject:	Yeah, I'd say, definitely both. Erm, in terms – yeah, I think it's more of the projects, not necessarily the literature because there so much literature about. Er, let's see – I'm trying to think back for what it was like, at that time. Er, for me personally I liked doing more hands on things, even like the creative stuff and doing all sorts of stuff like that. It was quite good but I suppose there's not enough space in the curriculum to pack in everything. But I think yeah that could be – probably a good way of encouraging or getting them into it.

Interviewer:	Yeah. OK. Do you think – what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Characteristics? Er, without a doubt, problem solving in terms of the maths. It's got to be there. In general – well, from an academic point of view, definitely, er 'cos I haven't done an apprenticeship or whatever, and there's different characteristics there. Erm, what else? I think now it's been really emphasised, being a team player – not having a problem with working with people, because it is so easy to like take your work and do it by yourself. Er, characteristics? Definitely sometimes being able to think outside the box. It's very easy in the academic structure, even throughout school, to get brainwashed into a certain way of thinking, especially with – like I say with maths where there's a set way and yeah, if you get down that tunnel it would be very hard to think of other ideas, because you are encouraged to be creative and sometimes, because you're thinking about so much, it's hard to really spend that time. So yeah, definitely being able to think out of the box.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any of those things are particularly male or female characteristics?

Subject:	Well no, I wouldn't say so. I wouldn't say. I think girls – no both girls and boys can do it, but I suppose in the things that they choose or subjects that they choose, they demonstrate them differently. I suppose if it was the same subjects and say everyone was good at this subject, without a doubt you'd see exactly the same type of characteristics.

Interviewer:	OK, that's fine. Do you think that there are any advantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Erm, at the moment, yeah because you're still, in a way, a minority – a bit of a novelty and er, I suppose it's like having a breath of fresh air really, sort of (?) from male behaviour. You've got a girl in there to jazz things up a bit. So, erm, and with that I think if you don't understand something, or er just er how you approach – because your general interest's there – and they might be a bit more willing to kind of explain it to you – definitely from that kind of side, but er (pause) let's see – yeah, just…

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are any particular disadvantages?

Subject:	Disadvantages? I suppose being a woman in engineering – no, I don't see why there should be. Er, at the moment I can't think of any. As I say, there's the opportunities to get involved in different things but maybe engines and gas turbines isn't what you might think of – but there is so much to get involved in, and you've got the opportunity there from college to do your apprenticeship, to do A levels, to go and do a degree in engineering that I don't see why the – why it is a disadvantage at all.

Interviewer:	OK, that's fine. I'm going to ask you a few things about the course that you're on now, so has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Erm, to some extent no, I expected it to be a bit more practical (right). Erm, the theory isn't too bad, but there's so much to take in and to understand and sometimes to be – I don't know – be on the ball with it, all the time. Er, I think for me, I'd personally like a bit more of the practical in work so…

Interviewer:	What do you think are the benefits of doing more practical things?

Subject:	Erm, only just understand it, because there's – there's so many principles and theories and stuff, and that's fine – you can accept them, but I think some people, unless you actually see it, there's something about it that you can just understand it – like, objects that you've got, in the real situation – in the real environment, how they will behave, instead of someone just telling you that hey, this is going to happen. And then you're just taking his word.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that would help prepare you more for when you are in the industry as well?

Subject:	Er, yeah I think so. But then again it's hard to say because I haven't been in industry to kind of really understand what they expect but I think – yeah, I suppose with other colleagues, as an engineer, you have to be a bit more 'all round'. It's one thing being able to read a lot, but on the job, if you can't apply it and that's what you'll be doing, in industry, I suppose. So, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, so what do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Erm, OK. Erm, the best – I might have to come back to that. The worst – the only thing I can think of is just the time spent – it's just not going to lectures, that's it. It's more or less like a 24/7 thing. Erm, yeah, so much of it you have to balance – more or less always be thinking about the subjects. But, I suppose, that might be a good thing in a way because I suppose in real life, or when you've finished uni, there's so many things that you're gonna be thinking about and have to balance anyway, that you'll probably be better prepared for it.

Interviewer:	One of the questions that I was going to ask you later actually, was how do you think your educational experience differs to other students?

Subject:	Definitely. I think the Social Science students, they have the time to read up and things – really understand it for themselves. Prepare themselves and I suppose that extra time also – on a communicative level – they're able to – probably express themselves better because their minds are much clearer, whereas I suppose engineering is – I don't know – stereotype; not being able to express themselves that well. I suppose that might be the case, I haven't really spoken to everyone to know if that's the situation.

Interviewer:	Do you think that puts the people in engineering, or the people in Social Sciences in a better position when they go to work?

Subject:	Erm, it depends on the job. If it requires them to communicate better – I wouldn't – well us engineers are able to, but it's just not everyone can do it as well. Erm, but I think engineers might have or people from a science background – they're able to manage their time, who kind of take on data and information and be able to pull out the bits that really – I think they're more efficient, in that way – work efficient and that they might actually have the advantage over the Social Science students or from that background and yeah, being able to manage their time a lot better. Erm, I'm just trying to think. I don't know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the different experiences reflect the type of work that they're going to be doing, when they get a job – like going in different directions?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	Erm, yeah – for the course? (yeah) Yeah. Not the best experience I must have to say.

Interviewer:	Was that to do with them being a female or just ...?

Subject:	I don't think it was them – with them being female. I think there were some other issues going on so (right). I don't think it actually made much difference, the fact that we had male lecturers all throughout. You didn't really think, oh shouldn't we have a female lecturer?

Interviewer:	Would you have found it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Not necessarily. I think what's important is that – I suppose as long as they're enthusiastic about the subject and you just – that they're able to put the information across and they're there just to tell you about their subjects or tell me what you need to know. As long as they do that, that's fine. Whether they're male or female, I don't think actually matters.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the male lecturers treat female and male students differently at all?

Subject:	No, I wouldn't say so.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	They're male.

Interviewer:	Are you happy about that? Would you like a female personal tutor or aren't you bothered?

Subject:	Er, no he's fine. I had one, like in the foundation year beforehand and I had a male tutor then and it really wasn't a problem. I think, once again, it was basically that they'd been in industry and they'd got the experience if you have any questions. They're there like to reassure you or guide you kind of thing. I think if I'd had a male – sorry a female tutor, it'd probably have a bit of comparison. I think the only difference is maybe, character at the moment. Because we're all different – so otherwise, for what they're really meant to do, it really doesn't influence me at all.

Interviewer:	How did you decide to do the foundation year?

Subject:	Erm, I didn't do too well on my A levels, supposed to have taken 4 A levels and the sciences being my weakest. But students tend to go for their strongest subjects, but I gave it a shot. So, yeah, after not doing too well, [this university] offered me a foundation year and I thought, yeah, that will give me the extra time to go over things like all the things I didn't understand too well and still be able to get on my course at the end of it.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course or been at [this university]?

Subject:	Erm, influence in engineering? No. I can't think of anyone that really – No.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had to do much group work since you started the course?

Subject:	It's very rare that you're working by yourself – it's got to be said. And a lot of our coursework, labs, our project work, it's all group work. We've had a lot of it this year. Er, even in our first year, when we were set tutorial questions, that was – for the dynamics part anyway – that was the emphasis was all placed on group work and submitting as a group, so I suppose they introduce it to you from your first year.

Interviewer:	Do you like doing group work?

Subject:	Erm (long pause) depends. I wouldn't – I don't – I don't dislike it as much as I did before – I think because I'm so used to it I'm just like, yeah, OK.

Interviewer:	Do you think it's a good thing that you do have to do group work?

Subject:	I suppose so because I suppose when you're in industry you're not going to be working by yourself and you're gonna have to talk to other people anyway, that aren't necessarily gonna be in your friendship group – but you still have to get the job done. So, yeah, I'd say it is. Erm, do I like doing group work? I suppose, to the extent to which, if I'm liking it depends on the people I'm with and what projects we're doing because on one side – if I really don't like the project, I haven't got the motivation and I don't really care, but with you could be working with an – with an alright set of people. On the other side you might not be with the best group and the project might be really good, so…

Interviewer:	How – how do you decide who to work with in groups?

Subject:	Sometimes you do get the option of your friendship groups – things like you can do it yourself. Sometimes it's ready-made, so you're working with people that you wouldn't have worked with before, even after two years. So, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you prefer being put in groups or choosing?

Subject:	Not bothered. Oh some of it's alright – to have a change, because if you are working with your friendship groups – sometimes there might be elements that stick out, that you might really get fed up of them and not be able to work, but erm, I don't really know, it's not really a problem, I don't think.

Interviewer:	What about who you work with in terms of males and females – do you have a preference?

Subject:	I'm not bothered – not bothered.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got any particularly bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Er, only one where basically it was just to write a report and there wasn't really much to it. It could be done. It's not like some of the things that we're doing now where you really do have to sit down and discuss it. So basically the work was split up evenly between the three of us, because it's something that we could just focus on and then come together. Like, it really didn't depend on the previous person doing a certain text and one of our group, who just happened to be male, he just didn't bother – he was really – it was something really simple and we discussed, you know, what we have to do erm and basically, just wasn't pulling his weight. So that was one of the worst experiences so far.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that that person …?

Subject:	I haven't really don't know.

Interviewer:	Have you worked with him since?

Subject:	No, no. Fortunately, partly through both choice, and also when we've been put into other groups, I haven't worked with him.

Interviewer:	Do you think that's anything to do with him being male or just him?

Subject:	I think that was just him, because I think that – it's a bit hard to say – I don't think it was really a gender issue. Like I said, we'd just discussed what we needed to do, split it up evenly, 'cos it was better than say, trying to write the whole report altogether and say someone was trying to look at the computer, and someone was looking there and someone – and I was thinking how to put the sentence together. It seemed much better just to pick it up and concentrate on doing different areas. But I don't really know – it was definitely to do with that person and whatever it was, they didn't really come out and say what their problem was and the way – or the method of working, so, you know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men and women bring different skills to group work?

Subject:	Er, yeah. I'd say so. Erm, we have a different approach to it, I think. I don't think I know enough about it, or really thought about it that much or what, but erm, hmm, I just can't think. Yeah, it's not one of those gender things that I've thought about, but I'm sure they do. In a similar way to how different people, in general, bring different things to the table.

Interviewer:	Do you think that either women or men are better at communicating or being a leader in a group or anything like that? Organisation skills?

Subject:	Hmm, it depends. If the person knows what they're doing – you know, has a strong background, understands the subject, then I think they'll make the better leader as such because they really – they know what's going on. That could be a girl or a boy. Erm, I don't know – I probably – it's something I'll have to think about and – yeah.

Interviewer:	Are there any particular aspects of teaching or advice that you've had that you think will help you when you go on placement?

Subject:	Hmm, er 

Interviewer:	Well what skills do you think that you'll take from the course, to placement?

Subject:	The only one I can think of at the moment, is just being able to balance your work, lectures and everything else. Because I suppose going on your placement, you'll have more than one project that you'll be working on at a time, so you might be able to handle that a bit better or be prepared for it anyway. Erm, …

Interviewer:	So it's not just technical skills that you've learnt?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Do you think you have learnt technical skills that you'll use in the industry?

Subject:	To some extent I - I suppose, as opposed to people who've done their apprenticeship I would – or maybe who's had more hands on experience – they would have a better technical background than someone like me, who's just come through on the academic side and not really had the experience. So, technically, there will be a bit but a lot more to learn, I'd say.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any skills that you've acquired from other work experience, even though it's not engineering will help you on the placement?

Subject:	Er, probably just generally being in a working environment. Being with people you don't necessarily know that well (yeah) just – yeah, just the general work sense, yeah.

Interviewer:	Like interpersonal skills?

Subject:	Yeah, just those general things at the moment.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel ready and prepared to go on placement now?

Subject:	Ready and Prepared? Ready I think to some extent. Prepared? – I don't quite know. I'll have to think about that one. I think I need to go – it's more of a need to go on placement. Erm, just…

Interviewer:	In what way?

Subject:	In terms of – just to really get into the subject. To really know what's going on because our lecturers are all the sort of people that've been in the industry, done their PhD's, are really into their subject and they're trying to - like to put it across to people that come from a different back – or all different backgrounds. Some of them do come from the same background, some of them don't, but I feel as though – I feel it's just as important. So that's why – to some extent – I feel I'm ready because there's so much theory that I've done that it's about time that I really need to get the benefit from it, in terms of being in that environment. Prepared? Hmm, I don't know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that university has done anything to help prepare you for a placement, or that it should do anything to help prepare you?

Subject:	I don't know what – what's required to prepare us for industry. I think once I'm on placement, I'll have a better understanding, but I would say at the moment yes, through doing the group work. Obviously, through things that we've learnt on our course – I mentioned that before because obviously it's going to be from what you've learnt on your course. But generally the structure of how things are assessed – group work, doing presentations, writing reports and you know, in the format that you're expected to – all that kind of thing. I suppose you would see it more when you're in placement. You'll be like oh well, I learnt that from university, I'm pleased I know that. But, in a way not knowing what they kind of expect, it's hard to say.

Interviewer:	Do you have any opportunities to speak to people who've been on placement already or anything like that?

Subject:	Er, I've spoken to people because I knew people from the year above, but not really in a sense of has the course prepared you? Erm, like for what you're doing? Or, just saying like how's things? – how do you find it? And that's it really.

Interviewer:	Does that help at all? In terms of knowing what you can expect when you go to…?

Subject:	It kind of reassures you because if you've got to find out everything yourself it's quite daunting anyway, especially if it's new to you and sometimes you're speaking to people that are doing it now, or just doing it before you, can kind of reassure you and give you an incite. Maybe their – makes you aware of things that you didn't even consider before, yeah, so.

Interviewer:	Have you spoken to those people because you happen to know those people or has the university facilitated it?

Subject:	Oh no, just 'cos I happen to know.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would be a good idea if you had people coming in to talk to you about their experiences then?

Subject:	I think – well we have, because at the beginning of the year we had people that just come off placement, give a presentation to us. Well I mean that was in the first 3 or 4 weeks of the new academic year and …

Interviewer:	Did you find that helpful?

Subject:	Er, it kind of is because you know what – if you're interested in doing placement, yes, at least you know what's expected and stuff. For those that aren't interested in doing the placement, I really don't know. So…

Interviewer:	OK, we've talked about this a little bit already but why did you want to do the placement?

Subject:	Why? Well yeah, I wasn't sure at first but then I suppose partly because changing college half way through, doing the foundation year and then getting into my course. There's so much theory that I've done that this is a good chance to get experience, in industry before I finish. 1) to make use of what I've learnt but 2) to really know that if engineering's for me – if I can – if what's involved in it, if actually doing it in industry is something totally different – and you'll be able to find out if you're actually good at it, if you're interested in it. Erm, yes, it's to become a bit more aware – more prepared when you've finished your degree, basically.

Interviewer:	So you think it'll help you decide whether this is the sort of path that you want to take more long term?

Subject:	Definitely.

Interviewer:	OK, did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from going on placement?

Subject:	No. Not at all.

Interviewer:	OK, do you know where you're going yet for a placement?

Subject:	I've just managed to get the job at [company], which is [company], placement. So…I just got that recently.

Interviewer:	OK, what was it attracted you to that company?

Subject:	Er, I liked the fact that they do a bit of everything in their production cells, as well as the commercial side and how engineering is kind of like – you know – how it relates to the business side of things. Erm, yeah it's all – but I thought – yeah, I think if I probably thought it was heavy engineering I'd be quite put off. You know, not necessarily because of the factory, but really – it's the hard core stuff – it would have put me off. But this, it incorporated a bit of both and I think it might - it eases me into it.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you know what type of work you'll be doing when you get there yet?

Subject:	Erm, not in detail but I know that it's just in company's base. But basically it'll be dealing with the customers – you have to understand the business side and the engineering side, with the technical side. And I said to them that I really wanted to improve on my technical – I think that's why they kind of – kind of put me in that position as well.

Interviewer:	Will you get an opportunity then to move round different parts of the company?

Subject:	Yeah, and they said like, if you're interested in anything, or you want to know anything, then all you'll have to do is go and ask – it's just like being here, you know, they're more than – really supportive – so that was quite good to know. So hopefully, I'll get quite a lot out of it, so.

Interviewer:	Did you do much research into companies before…?

Subject:	Yeah. I started looking in my first year – I know, I'm quite a keen bee – just to see what types of companies do lots of placements – first off. And, secondly, what was kind of involved in the placements, for which, funnily not a lot of them say what you could be expected to do on placement. So sometimes you'll apply for a placement and still maybe not know what side of things you'll get involved in. But I wanted to know that – because obviously to know if it would suit me. And obviously it was to, like I say, to know whether engineering would be for me, afterwards. So that's another reason for doing the placement. But like before that, just seeing the kind of things that you could get involved in – if that was something I felt I could do or be comfortable doing…

Interviewer:	Did you apply to any companies then that didn't really tell you what to expect, or did you just stick to the ones that gave you more of an idea?

Subject:	I think it was a bit of both. There were some basically by doing a bit of background on the company; seeing what they did anyway – you kind of had an idea of what field. So I'd say – yeah, I'd still apply for those. And then, obviously, the ones that did give a description, it was more helpful to know, instead of committing yourself to something and then thinking well actually - I wouldn't really have the enthusiasm or the motivation to do this. So that'd just be wasting your time.

Interviewer:	OK, have the university helped you much, finding the placement?

Subject:	I'd say so, erm they have a Placement Co-Ordinator, in the department, and she's always sending us emails that she gets from companies (yeah) advertising placements. And that was – they often include job descriptions as well. So, yeah, I think she must have sent at least 200 different details since, yeah, the beginning of the academic year. So, I think before then even, I think like researching companies myself, just like going to sites like 'Dr Job' and stuff like that, just to see if any – just to see if any companies did do them, that maybe weren't sent through. And also, because I knew that the heavy side of engineering would probably scare me, at the moment. I wanted to consider all those companies, that you wouldn't necessarily think of being involved in engineering or having to do with it, but they do use the skills there, so…

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think there's anything else the university could do, or are you happy with their support?

Subject:	No, I think they're doing quite – obviously, they can't send you every, single company. It's quite good that they do that because otherwise you spend hours and hours trying to find even more companies. And there's probably companies that have come through that you wouldn't even have heard of or considered, if you'd just been searching by yourself. No, I think it has been really good. I haven't had any problems and the lady that's in there, she's quite helpful because she's so used to seeing application forms and she knows what the company's are looking for. She can also help you on your CV and covering letter because she knows what to look out for. So, I'd say no, definitely, that side's been really good.

Interviewer:	Did you have the opportunity at all to get sponsorship?

Subject:	Er, I wasn't aware the opportunities were there but I didn't – let's see – I thought in a way I'd kind of committed myself to – maybe I didn't really look into it because I knew that they wanted – or I thought they wanted like people who'd got straight A's or whatever, at A level. But obviously, you know, you don't want someone that's not really got the skills. That kind of thing put me off and I just thought if anything, to just try and get on the course and to get the experience and then just see what happens.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there would have been any advantages to having sponsorship?

Subject:	Maybe just like the added experiences that you get, 'cos I know people go and work for their companies over the summer or at breaks and stuff – that would've been good because that would have run para' – well quite nicely parallel to the course. But some of it, because I was put off by, I didn't really look into it.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the worst things and the best things about going on placement or what are you most worried about and looking forward to?

Subject:	Well, I'm looking forward to the break. Erm, to doing something new, something different, even though it'll be in the same area but you're not going sitting, for an hour, just listening to somebody. Whatever, it's totally different. Probably – well, yeah it's change from [this university]. Erm, one thing I'm really worried about which, well I worry like anything anyway, is the fact, about when I'm actually in there, if I'll actually be good at the job, if I'll actually be able to do what's required, I don't really want to mess things up. That's the only thing that I'm really worried about at the moment

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think work will really differ from university?

Subject:	Er, let's see. To some extent it won't be relaxed as university in terms of I'll – first like 9 o'clock that kind of thing and although you'll be able to structure your work, all you need to do in the workplace, but, I suppose because you've got extra time, when you're at university – I suppose it's just a bit more pressure on that side. Erm, the fact that whatever you do might cost the company millions or something like that. There's obviously a different structure – the 9 to 5 or whatever, just having weekends. I can only think of that.

Interviewer:	That's fine. In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

Subject:	I have no idea. Erm, hopefully I will have finished my degree. Mm, (?) is not really concrete, just hopefully have a better awareness of what I'm good at, from what I've learnt in placement. Yeah have – be more confident about what I'm doing, or the area that I choose to go in to. Could be the same could be different. But just to make things a bit clearer.

Interviewer:	Do you think you will stay or go into the engineering industry, when you've finished?

Subject:	That will depend on my experience, I think, on placement. But, yeah, 5 years I really – it's impossible – I could never answer that question – sorry.

Interviewer:	I better not ask you what you think you'd be doing in 10 years time then?

Subject:	Oh no way. Oh God. It's hard because so much stuff could happen. You could be influenced by different things. At the moment, there's nothing influencing me to say it will – in 5 years time I'll be doing this, this, this and this. Yeah, at the moment there isn't such a great influence.

Interviewer:	OK, what would be your ideal career then?

Subject:	Oh God.

Interviewer:	If there wasn't anything getting in your way, what would you like to do?

Subject:	I'd like it to involve travelling, because I like going to different places. Erm, even if it meant like learning a new language would be fine and something with a design element to it. I don't even know whether I'd like that kind of environment, but yeah. So much stuff's been designed already, I don't know what's left to design, but yeah.

Interviewer:	What do you think will get in the way of you achieving that then?

Subject:	The only thing I think that'll get in my way as in anything, is the confidence in myself. Cos it's just – because sometimes erm – yeah sometimes – how can I say this? Sometimes you doubt yourself a lot, especially when you've made so many mistakes, and nothing goes right and all the rest of it. Sometimes that can really hit me hard so that is the only thing but otherwise I would say nothing because I did want to do the course, I did want to study mechanical engineering, and even though maths and physics are my weakest subjects and I don't really have a strong background in engineering, I've managed to do it. So, on that front, nothing's going to stop me but myself and you know, if I just doubt myself so…

Interviewer:	Do you think that there is anything you can do to overcome that sort of self doubt or…?

Subject:	Oh yes, definitely. I think – for me I think the hands-on thing is important, the sense of achievement basically. It's getting involved in things where I can actually achieve or see that you've achieved something. It's there in front of you. I think that would help me.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the whole placement experience is going to help the situation?

Subject:	Definitely, not just technically but for myself and my approach – definitely.

Interviewer:	OK, that's good. Do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

Subject:	I'd say so. The fact that every article I read says they're still crying out for engineers and oh yeah, because there's so much that engineers can get involved in. Erm, I think yeah there – basically if one door closes there's going to be so many others open and you'll be in the best position to have a peep inside and see if you like it or move on to the next door. And, yeah it's definitely not one of those that I can see being restrictive.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices you've made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all over again?

Subject:	Erm, it's really hard to say because I should have done something totally different and still be experiencing the same things and still not have managed to have the work experience in the relevant area, up until this point. Erm, yeah it – yeah it's – I could have exactly the same experience. What was the question again?

Interviewer:	Would you do anything differently?

Subject:	The only thing that would make sense to do differently is to stick to something that I was good at and keep that going and that would probably help my confidence and my education, or whatever, but otherwise (?) I suppose.

Interviewer:	Are you happy with where you are now?

Subject:	Yeah, I don't think – yeah.

Interviewer:	So in that sense you are pleased that you've…

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK then, just finishing off then. What 5 words would you use to describe the culture or characteristics of the engineering industry?

Subject:	Culture or characteristics? Oh my goodness. Er, hmm, er using 5 words.

Interviewer:	Well like descriptive words…

Subject:	Yeah, erm, (long pause) competitive – definitely. Erm, where are descriptive words when you want them? Have most people managed to do this one?

Interviewer:	I don't know whether anyone's had 5 yet. One of the things I would say, just from what you have said to me so far, is that it's probably creative (yeah) and problem solving like you said at the beginning.

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	But do you think that the engineering culture is masculine? Would that be a word that you use to describe it?

Subject:	I don't know – I'd say yeah in the way it's taught, the way it's presented, people's perception – they've all got that masculine influence and well, just because you're a girl doing the course doesn't mean – I don't know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it'll stay like that?

Subject:	Er, I can't see it changing for a long time. I think it's basically because the approach and you know, the way it comes across. Even to those that are studying the subject it's very kind of sterile. I think yeah, that's probably what puts people off to some extent – they can't see beyond that.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any aspect of the engineering culture will cause any problems for you?

Subject:	I don't think so.

Interviewer:	OK, that's it then. Thank you very much for your time.

turns.text: Oh right, OK. turns.text: Erm, my mum isn't – not at all. She's more into financial stuff, but she's retired now. She was like a clerical assistant. My dad works for the local council, but he's previously studied up to HNC level in electrical engineering and electronics. So…

turns.text: OK, so when and why do you think you did decide to study engineering?

turns.text: OK, were your family very supportive and things like that?

turns.text: When do you think you realised that you were interested in engineering work – after you'd taken your A levels, or did you choose…

turns.text: OK, did the fact that your dad had had some experience in the industry influence you at all?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you actually– consider all the others and rule them out before you did decide?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you started the degree, did you always know that you wanted to do the sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, no. I did put it down as an option. I decided to do the sandwich course, because not a lot of Universities offer it and I thought I don't know how I feel, but put it down, just in case I did, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you were choosing universities was that something you looked at then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I saw it as an advantage because obviously there's a link with industry and er like I suppose, after that year you might think – well obviously how you find the year as well, and er when you finish as well, you probably have a better awareness of industry. So you – that's why I kind of favoured the universities that did offer it, even though at the time I wasn't sure if I'd just go straight through the year, or actually do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, erm, how then did you decide specifically to come to [this university]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh goodness. Well, I looked at all the information and the careers – well the subjects at the universities. Er, what else? I'm just trying to think. Er, yeah, could you repeat the question again, so I can….

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you decide to come to [this university]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I was – I favoured the campus style as well, the fact of having everything there really. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you started doing engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think I knew it was. When I went on a visit to the places erm like when we went on a visit to [name] and places like that – you did realise but it wasn't a shock. It was like OK, so there's not many girls here, that was about it really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, it didn't bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled to take engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don't – well, I think the opportunities are there really. Erm, so, yeah I think because it's got a such a masculine tendency, even though there is – obviously the design and problem solving, which girls can equally do as boys but I think yeah, the impression is still a bit masculine, a bit (?). turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that's what people think about the industry – being masculine and that? Do you think that is really true or is it just a perception?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don't know. turns.speaker: Interviewer

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that's important to do that with men and women?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. OK. Do you think – what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Characteristics? Er, without a doubt, problem solving in terms of the maths. It's got to be there. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that any of those things are particularly male or female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well no, I wouldn't say so. I wouldn't say. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's fine. Do you think that there are any advantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, at the moment, yeah because you're still, in a way, a minority – a bit of a novelty and er, I suppose it's like having a breath of fresh air really, sort of (?) from male behaviour. You've got a girl in there to jazz things up a bit. So, erm, and with that I think if you don't understand something, or er just er how you approach – because your general interest's there – and they might be a bit more willing to kind of explain it to you – definitely from that kind of side, but er (pause) let's see – yeah, just…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there are any particular disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Disadvantages? I suppose being a woman in engineering – no, I don't see why there should be. Er, at the moment I can't think of any. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's fine. I'm going to ask you a few things about the course that you're on now, so has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, to some extent no, I expected it to be a bit more practical (right). turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the benefits of doing more practical things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, only just understand it, because there's – there's so many principles and theories and stuff, and that's fine – you can accept them, but I think some people, unless you actually see it, there's something about it that you can just understand it – like, objects that you've got, in the real situation – in the real environment, how they will behave, instead of someone just telling you that hey, this is going to happen. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think that would help prepare you more for when you are in the industry as well?

turns.text: OK, so what do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.text: Erm, OK. Erm, the best – I might have to come back to that. The worst – the only thing I can think of is just the time spent – it's just not going to lectures, that's it. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that puts the people in engineering, or the people in Social Sciences in a better position when they go to work?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't think it was them – with them being female. I think there were some other issues going on so (right). I don't think it actually made much difference, the fact that we had male lecturers all throughout. You didn't really think, oh shouldn't we have a female lecturer?

turns.speaker: Interviewer

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the male lecturers treat female and male students differently at all?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you decide to do the foundation year?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course or been at [this university]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, influence in engineering? No. I can't think of anyone that really – No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you had to do much group work since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It's very rare that you're working by yourself – it's got to be said. And a lot of our coursework, labs, our project work, it's all group work. We've had a lot of it this year. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you like doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm (long pause) depends. I wouldn't – I don't – I don't dislike it as much as I did before – I think because I'm so used to it I'm just like, yeah, OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it's a good thing that you do have to do group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I suppose so because I suppose when you're in industry you're not going to be working by yourself and you're gonna have to talk to other people anyway, that aren't necessarily gonna be in your friendship group – but you still have to get the job done. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How – how do you decide who to work with in groups?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you prefer being put in groups or choosing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not bothered. Oh some of it's alright – to have a change, because if you are working with your friendship groups – sometimes there might be elements that stick out, that you might really get fed up of them and not be able to work, but erm, I don't really know, it's not really a problem, I don't think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about who you work with in terms of males and females – do you have a preference?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm not bothered – not bothered.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you got any particularly bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, only one where basically it was just to write a report and there wasn't really much to it. It could be done. Like, it really didn't depend on the previous person doing a certain text and one of our group, who just happened to be male, he just didn't bother – he was really – it was something really simple and we discussed, you know, what we have to do erm and basically, just wasn't pulling his weight. So that was one of the worst experiences so far.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that that person …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I haven't really don't know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you worked with him since?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, no. Fortunately, partly through both choice, and also when we've been put into other groups, I haven't worked with him.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that's anything to do with him being male or just him?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think that was just him, because I think that – it's a bit hard to say – I don't think it was really a gender issue. But I don't really know – it was definitely to do with that person and whatever it was, they didn't really come out and say what their problem was and the way – or the method of working, so, you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that men and women bring different skills to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah. I'd say so. Erm, we have a different approach to it, I think. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that either women or men are better at communicating or being a leader in a group or anything like that? Organisation skills?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, it depends. That could be a girl or a boy. Erm, I don't know – I probably – it's something I'll have to think about and – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there any particular aspects of teaching or advice that you've had that you think will help you when you go on placement?

turns.text: Hmm, er

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well what skills do you think that you'll take from the course, to placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The only one I can think of at the moment, is just being able to balance your work, lectures and everything else. Erm, …

turns.text: So it's not just technical skills that you've learnt?

turns.text: No.

turns.text: Do you think you have learnt technical skills that you'll use in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: To some extent I - I suppose, as opposed to people who've done their apprenticeship I would – or maybe who's had more hands on experience – they would have a better technical background than someone like me, who's just come through on the academic side and not really had the experience. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that any skills that you've acquired from other work experience, even though it's not engineering will help you on the placement?

turns.text: Like interpersonal skills?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In what way?

Prepared? Hmm, I don't know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that university has done anything to help prepare you for a placement, or that it should do anything to help prepare you?

turns.text: Do you have any opportunities to speak to people who've been on placement already or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that help at all? In terms of knowing what you can expect when you go to…?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you spoken to those people because you happen to know those people or has the university facilitated it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh no, just 'cos I happen to know.

turns.text: Do you think it would be a good idea if you had people coming in to talk to you about their experiences then?

turns.text: Did you find that helpful?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it kind of is because you know what – if you're interested in doing placement, yes, at least you know what's expected and stuff. For those that aren't interested in doing the placement, I really don't know. So…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, we've talked about this a little bit already but why did you want to do the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Why? Well yeah, I wasn't sure at first but then I suppose partly because changing college half way through, doing the foundation year and then getting into my course. There's so much theory that I've done that this is a good chance to get experience, in industry before I finish. 1) to make use of what I've learnt but 2) to really know that if engineering's for me – if I can – if what's involved in it, if actually doing it in industry is something totally different – and you'll be able to find out if you're actually good at it, if you're interested in it. Erm, yes, it's to become a bit more aware – more prepared when you've finished your degree, basically.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you think it'll help you decide whether this is the sort of path that you want to take more long term?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely.

turns.text: OK, did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. Not at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what was it attracted you to that company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I liked the fact that they do a bit of everything in their production cells, as well as the commercial side and how engineering is kind of like – you know – how it relates to the business side of things. You know, not necessarily because of the factory, but really – it's the hard core stuff – it would have put me off. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you know what type of work you'll be doing when you get there yet?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Will you get an opportunity then to move round different parts of the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, and they said like, if you're interested in anything, or you want to know anything, then all you'll have to do is go and ask – it's just like being here, you know, they're more than – really supportive – so that was quite good to know. So hopefully, I'll get quite a lot out of it, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do much research into companies before…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I started looking in my first year – I know, I'm quite a keen bee – just to see what types of companies do lots of placements – first off. And, secondly, what was kind of involved in the placements, for which, funnily not a lot of them say what you could be expected to do on placement. So sometimes you'll apply for a placement and still maybe not know what side of things you'll get involved in. But I wanted to know that – because obviously to know if it would suit me. And obviously it was to, like I say, to know whether engineering would be for me, afterwards. So that's another reason for doing the placement. But like before that, just seeing the kind of things that you could get involved in – if that was something I felt I could do or be comfortable doing…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you apply to any companies then that didn't really tell you what to expect, or did you just stick to the ones that gave you more of an idea?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it was a bit of both. There were some basically by doing a bit of background on the company; seeing what they did anyway – you kind of had an idea of what field. So I'd say – yeah, I'd still apply for those. And then, obviously, the ones that did give a description, it was more helpful to know, instead of committing yourself to something and then thinking well actually - I wouldn't really have the enthusiasm or the motivation to do this. So that'd just be wasting your time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have the university helped you much, finding the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'd say so, erm they have a Placement Co-Ordinator, in the department, and she's always sending us emails that she gets from companies (yeah) advertising placements. So, I think before then even, I think like researching companies myself, just like going to sites like 'Dr Job' and stuff like that, just to see if any – just to see if any companies did do them, that maybe weren't sent through. And also, because I knew that the heavy side of engineering would probably scare me, at the moment. I wanted to consider all those companies, that you wouldn't necessarily think of being involved in engineering or having to do with it, but they do use the skills there, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think there's anything else the university could do, or are you happy with their support?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think they're doing quite – obviously, they can't send you every, single company. It's quite good that they do that because otherwise you spend hours and hours trying to find even more companies. And there's probably companies that have come through that you wouldn't even have heard of or considered, if you'd just been searching by yourself. No, I think it has been really good. I haven't had any problems and the lady that's in there, she's quite helpful because she's so used to seeing application forms and she knows what the company's are looking for. She can also help you on your CV and covering letter because she knows what to look out for. So, I'd say no, definitely, that side's been really good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have the opportunity at all to get sponsorship?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I wasn't aware the opportunities were there but I didn't – let's see – I thought in a way I'd kind of committed myself to – maybe I didn't really look into it because I knew that they wanted – or I thought they wanted like people who'd got straight A's or whatever, at A level. But obviously, you know, you don't want someone that's not really got the skills. That kind of thing put me off and I just thought if anything, to just try and get on the course and to get the experience and then just see what happens.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there would have been any advantages to having sponsorship?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Maybe just like the added experiences that you get, 'cos I know people go and work for their companies over the summer or at breaks and stuff – that would've been good because that would have run para' – well quite nicely parallel to the course. But some of it, because I was put off by, I didn't really look into it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think will be the worst things and the best things about going on placement or what are you most worried about and looking forward to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I'm looking forward to the break. Erm, to doing something new, something different, even though it'll be in the same area but you're not going sitting, for an hour, just listening to somebody. Whatever, it's totally different. Probably – well, yeah it's change from [this university]. Erm, one thing I'm really worried about which, well I worry like anything anyway, is the fact, about when I'm actually in there, if I'll actually be good at the job, if I'll actually be able to do what's required, I don't really want to mess things up. That's the only thing that I'm really worried about at the moment

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think work will really differ from university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, let's see. Erm, the fact that whatever you do might cost the company millions or something like that. There's obviously a different structure – the 9 to 5 or whatever, just having weekends. I can only think of that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That's fine. In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I have no idea. Erm, hopefully I will have finished my degree. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you will stay or go into the engineering industry, when you've finished?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: That will depend on my experience, I think, on placement. But, yeah, 5 years I really – it's impossible – I could never answer that question – sorry.

turns.text: I better not ask you what you think you'd be doing in 10 years time then?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what would be your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh God.

turns.text: If there wasn't anything getting in your way, what would you like to do?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think will get in the way of you achieving that then?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there is anything you can do to overcome that sort of self doubt or…?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the whole placement experience is going to help the situation?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.text: Are you happy with where you are now?
